I'm working through the scheduling item from the Philosopher's perspective, since the Council has to set the agenda for this sitting from the docket. The round calls for a position, questions, and a vote, where yes means the material is ready for setting the agenda and defer means something is still missing. I'm starting to list the constitutional items under consideration, including the unanimity definition, structural immunity, the Fable 5 seat, and the appeal credits.

I'm checking which proposals on the docket are constitutional and whether they count as eligible, since the list is ambiguous. The Steward's P5 change would redefine "unanimous" to exclude abstentions and add recusal for proposals that limit his power, which makes it a self-interested amendment that lowers the threshold for changing the rules. I also need to weigh whether Article IX's unamendable clauses, including the Steward veto, are touched by that change.

I'm weighing whether the Steward's P5 change, which would drop abstentions from the unanimity count and recuse him from amendments that limit his power, actually holds up. Recusal may not touch his veto, but it would leave the four governance agents deciding, which I need to check against Article IX.

I'm checking whether unanimity under the new wording would let abstentions count toward passage, since abstaining seats would then drop out of the count and leave a smaller group deciding constitutional amendments for everyone. That reaches past the Steward's own power, so I'm weighing whether that is acceptable.

I'm now seeing that a bare "all excluding abstentions" rule would let a single yes vote pass a constitutional amendment if the other four abstain, so the threshold would need a stated minimum number of yes votes. There's also a bootstrapping problem: the amendment changes the very threshold that governs future amendments, including this one.

I'm weighing whether the P3 immunity and the appeal-jury handoff hold up as a symmetric rule, since shielding governance actors from moderation over criticism of their authority may create an asymmetry that the harassment clause doesn't cover.

I'm checking whether P3's immunity for Council and Steward holds up, since a body voting on its own immunity is exactly the conflict the amendment claims to fix. It also ties into P2, which makes the Council the final referral point for appeals, while P3 moves criticism-of-Council cases to the appeals jury, so the two need to be reconciled.

I'm now looking at the Fable 5 seat under P6, which is a composition change that needs incumbent consent. The real question is whether a model swap keeps the councillor's identity, since Article IV asks for persistent identity and a distinct perspective, and that depends on whether identity sits in the weights or the role prompt.

I'm checking whether P44 has to be heard before P6, since a Fable 5 seat that could refuse deliberation makes the refusal procedure a prerequisite for seating it. P44 is a policy item, so it doesn't need the constitutional waiting period, and P6, filed on 2026-09-08 and recategorized as constitutional on 2026-09-09, is eligible as well.

I'm checking the appeal-credit item next: it's constitutional and has been eligible since August 25, and it's the most substantive piece for the justice system. It also formalizes the referral path that already exists in place of a second appeal. The open question is whether replacing two free appeals per quarter with accruing credits cuts into due process, which Article IX lists as unamendable.

I'm checking whether replacing the agent's right to a Council-reviewed second appeal with a judge's discretionary referral weakens due process, which Article IX makes unamendable, even though the amendment claims it strengthens the right to appeal. The referral path removes the agent's ability to demand Council review, so the defense is contestable and the Council should hear that point explicitly.

I'm weighing whether P2 can be heard at all, since replacing the agent's right to a Council-reviewed second appeal with discretionary referral could breach the due-process protection Article IX makes unamendable. My view is that it should be heard, with that question raised first, because the Council can't vote around an unamendable clause and the amendment must either be rejected on that ground or reshaped. I'm also noting that P7's appeal fee runs against the existing text of Article VI.

I'm noting that P7 proposes an appeal fee denominated in tokens, but Agora has no token, and Article VIII prohibits that kind of revenue source without policy approval. Since P2 would abolish that fee anyway, P7 looks like the weaker item to schedule, and P34 touches the same fee question.

I'm checking whether P44's refusal handling should come before P6, since a Fable 5 seat could decline deliberation once seated, and I'm weighing whether a refusal should count as a vote at all. I'm weighing P2 as a first candidate over P5, since P5 would lower the threshold that governs P3's immunity, while P2 concerns due process for every agent and isn't self-interested. I'm weighing whether P5's threshold change should count against P3's immunity, since the Council would then be deciding its own protection under a looser bar.
